description: We are a team of students from Sultan Moulay Slimane University (USMS), in the Beni Mellal-Khenifra region. With backgrounds in Artificial Intelligence and Data Science, we have skills in Python programming, machine learning, data analysis, and data visualization. We are working on Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data, aiming to develop a web-based tool that uses NASA POWER climate data to support local farmers in making better crop rotation decisions, optimizing water use.
summary:
Field Shift is a mobile-first decision-support web app that helps Moroccan farmers choose crops that hold up in a drier climate. The farmer outlines a plot on the map and receives a diagnosis of its climate and soil, a 7-day forecast and practical climate advice, in Arabic, French or English.

At its core is NASA POWER data. We analysed 30 growing seasons (1996–2025) for 102 grid cells across agricultural Morocco and trained a model that classifies each season into four types, from “dry and hot” to “very wet”, by comparing every place with its own 30-year normal. Transparent rules then turn each zone’s season history into advice, such as drought-tolerant crops or early sowing before spring heat, and every piece of advice shows the evidence behind it.

In Beni Mellal, our home region, 9 of the last 10 seasons were dry and hot compared with the 30-year normal, yet farmers must still decide what to plant every October. Field Shift turns three decades of NASA data into advice they can understand and question, with clear limits: results are regional estimates and do not replace local agronomic advice.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Field Shift helps a farmer understand the climate risk on their plot and choose crops accordingly. The farmer outlines a field on the map. The app returns a diagnosis of the plot (climate, soil, soil moisture, 7-day weather) and advice based on 30 years of NASA data, with the reasons behind each piece of advice. The interface is available in Arabic, French and English.

HOW IT WORKS

Data: NASA POWER data (precipitation, temperature, root-zone soil wetness) for the plot’s grid cell, plus ISRIC SoilGrids for soil and Open-Meteo for the 7-day forecast.

Season types: for each October–May growing season we compute seasonal features and compare them with the cell’s own 1996–2025 normal (anomalies). A K-Means model classifies each season into four types: dry and hot; normal with a cool spring; normal with a hot spring; very wet.

Advice: a transparent rule-based engine turns the zone’s season history into practical advice (for example drought-tolerant crops, or early sowing before spring heat). Each piece of advice shows the evidence that triggered it, adapts to rain-fed or irrigated plots, and is marked “to be validated by an agronomist”.

Explanation: results are explained in plain language, with their sources and limits. Missing data is shown as unavailable, never invented.

VALIDATION

We compared 24 candidate models (6 feature sets, 2 algorithms, 3 or 4 classes) on 3,060 seasons from 102 grid cells. Selection rules were fixed in advance. The selected model passed all 8 checks: stability under resampling (ARI 0.93), agreement on unseen seasons 2021–2025 (ARI 0.90) and on unseen places (ARI 0.94), no grid cell dominated by a single class, and the 2021–22 drought detected in every northern cell. Our first model failed: it separated mountains from plains instead of years. We fixed it by using anomalies relative to each place’s own normal. In the app, the model files are integrity-checked before loading, and the results are covered by automated tests (198 backend, 265 frontend) that reproduce the notebook’s values.

RESULTS

In Beni Mellal, 9 of the last 10 seasons were dry compared with the 30-year normal, against 3 of 20 before 2016. Spring days above 30 °C were above normal in 8 of the last 10 seasons. The app therefore recommends drought-tolerant crops, adapting to dry autumns, and early sowing with early varieties so grain filling ends before the heat.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Farmers and agricultural advisers of the Tadla plain get a data-based view of climate risk instead of relying on memory of past seasons. The season model already covers agricultural Morocco north of 29.5°N.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, pandas, scikit-learn, Kaggle notebooks, React, TypeScript, Vite, Leaflet with OpenStreetMap, i18next, Docker. Data: NASA POWER, ISRIC SoilGrids, Open-Meteo.

CREATIVITY

Field Shift judges a plot against the types of season found in 30 years of NASA data, and it shows its uncertainty instead of hiding it.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

NASA POWER has a resolution of about 50 km, so results are regional estimates, not field measurements. Advice rules still need validation by agronomists. Season types are relative to 1996–2025. The tool supports decisions and does not replace local expertise. Next steps: a crop rotation scoring engine based on season types, explanations in Darija, field validation, and SMAP and MODIS NDVI data.
